judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2017, which would have closed voting centers and cut back early voting sites. A voting center lets any voter in the county vote there rather than at one assigned polling place. County supervisors could no longer have authorized them. The law letting a county recorder set up on-site early voting places would have been repealed, and no precinct could have held more than 1,000 registered voters. The Arizona House passed it 32-26, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2438, which would have stopped a person changing the sex recorded on their birth certificate. Existing law allows the change after sex reassignment surgery, or where a chromosome count differs from the recorded sex, and both routes would have gone. Any other correction would have required proof of factual error beyond a reasonable doubt, the standard used in criminal trials. The Arizona Senate passed it 17-13, and the Governor vetoed it.

Certifying the count is the step that makes a result final. Other election offenses could still have been prosecuted. The Arizona House passed it 33-24, and the Governor vetoed it.

Card payment networks could not have used a separate merchant code to mark out gun retailers. The Arizona House passed it 32-25, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1164, which would have pushed local officials toward federal immigration enforcement. State and local officials could have worked with federal immigration agents. Jails would have had to act on immigration detainers. A detainer is a request to hold someone so federal agents can come for them. The Attorney General could have investigated and enforced compliance. The Arizona House passed it 33-26, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1256, which would have barred state agencies, boards and commissions using diversity, equity and inclusion programs when hiring, training or promoting staff. They could not have required an employee to take part in one, or made taking part a condition of a contract. The Department of Administration would have monitored hiring to enforce it. The Arizona House passed it 33-25, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1268, which would have made hospitals ask patients about their immigration status. Any hospital taking payment from the state health program would have had to put a space on its admission form for the patient, or their representative, to say whether they are a United States citizen, lawfully present, or not lawfully present. The health department would have reported the answers every three months. The Arizona House passed it 32-25, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1280, which would have required counties to send the cast vote record to the Secretary of State within 48 hours of the county count. A cast vote record is the anonymous list of how each ballot was marked. It would have had to go unaltered and in its original order, and would have become a public record. Precincts with under 25 registered voters would have been left out. The Arizona House passed it 33-25, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1584, which would have required the state and local government to hire on merit and nothing else. They also could not have shaped the make-up of their workforce by race, ethnicity, sex or national origin. The one exception was keeping hiring color-blind under existing anti-discrimination law. The Attorney General, a county attorney or any person could have gone to court to enforce it. The Arizona House passed it 31-21, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1586, which would have made a clinician personally liable for the cost of reversing gender transition care given to a minor. The liability would have been strict, so fault would not have had to be shown. It would have lasted 25 years after the original care. A person who later had reversal treatment could have sued until they turned 26. The Arizona House passed it 31-27, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1610, which would have required county jails to feed information to federal immigration agents. For people arrested on listed offenses, a jail would have had to send the name, address, date of birth, sex and social security number daily or on request. It would also have had to hand over a photograph and description, and allow an interview. The Arizona House passed it 33-25, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1694, which would have cut off all state money to any public university or community college that offers a course on diversity, equity and inclusion. The ban would have applied for the whole financial year in which such a course was offered. The state treasurer, the board of regents and the Department of Administration would all have been barred from paying the institution. The Arizona House passed it 32-23, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1705, which would have let a court fine a local official personally for making local gun rules. Arizona reserves firearm regulation to the state. An elected or appointed local official, or an agency head, who knowingly and willfully broke that rule could have been fined up to $5,000. The Arizona House passed it 31-24, and the Governor vetoed it.
